edges.description: Expressed in cultured endothelial cells and melanocytes, the mutant made the cells independent of growth factors by upregulating MAPK signalling; the steps from there to the tumour's lymphatic-type endothelium are not established. A later series found no GNA14 mutation in five further KHEs, and the 2020 review leaves open whether such mutations cause the tumour.

The nodules infiltrate across tissue planes, into the dermis, fat, muscle and bone. In mouse haemangioendothelioma cells, overexpression of PROX1 induced an invasive phenotype in vivo, a model of a link between the lymphatic programme and infiltration rather than a study of human tumours.
In most patients the infiltrating tumour presents as a soft-tissue mass with skin findings.
Pain can come from the infiltrating, destructive growth.
The infiltrating tumour invades the joints near it.

In a cohort selected for loss of joint motion, most limb lesions were on or next to large joints. The cohort calls the cause uncertain and, citing earlier work, states that infiltration of muscle, connective tissue and joint structures can lead to fibrosis and contracture.
The tumour invades and destroys bone.

Lymphoedema can follow the tumour, more often when it is large (10 cm or more), mixed and in a limb. On lymphoscintigraphy of 25 patients, 24 of them with a limb tumour, lymphatic stasis within the involved lesion was found in all 22 with abnormal findings, and lymphoedema was on the side of the lesion, as it was in all 13 affected patients of the cohort of 118. The 2020 review suggests that a tumour of the proximal limb, particularly at or near the inguinal or axillary lymph nodes, may influence lymphatic development or damage the lymphatic vessels, and reports a hypothesis that, for such tumours, obstruction of lymphatic flow during the acute Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon may lead to lymphoedema; it adds that inflammation may also play a role. In the cohort of 118, of whom 13 had lymphoedema, a history of the phenomenon and sirolimus treatment were not significant predictors of lymphoedema; with 13 cases this does not exclude them. The lymphoscintigraphy series' abstract names no centre, so whether it shares patients with the cohort of 118 is not known.

The tumour vasculature traps platelets. In 107 referrals, infiltration into muscle or deeper, and a retroperitoneal or intrathoracic site, were associated with a higher likelihood of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. In a series of 146 patients, mixed lesions (a cutaneous lesion with deep infiltration) had about four times the odds of the phenomenon that superficial ones had, in the univariate analysis.
Trapping and consumption of platelets lowers the platelet count.

Anaemia accompanies the falling platelet count of the phenomenon. The cited sources name the anaemia of the phenomenon as microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, and intralesional haemorrhage among its consequences, without tracing the steps from trapping to anaemia.

nodes.description: Ticlopidine and aspirin, which inhibit platelet aggregation, have been used in the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon: ticlopidine with aspirin, and ticlopidine with vincristine. The 2020 review gives ticlopidine by mouth at 10 mg/kg a day, recommends vincristine with aspirin, ticlopidine or both for the severe Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, and advises against ticlopidine alone in the phenomenon; the VASCERN-VASCA pathway notes that some centres use them despite a lack of evidence in the literature, and although platelet function is already impaired in the phenomenon. The phenomenon's own treatment is curated in the Kasabach-Merritt Syndrome entry.

nodes.description: Recommended as a first-line treatment of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon because they raise the platelet count quickly; given alone, many cases do not improve, with response rates of 10 to 27%. The 2020 review gives oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg a day or intravenous methylprednisolone 1.6 mg/kg a day, and recommends them for the severe Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon together with vincristine or sirolimus. One cohort's discussion describes starting methylprednisolone at 2 to 3 mg/kg a day for less than a week, and says 5 to 6 mg/kg a day can be used for extremely low platelet counts and life-threatening conditions; its results report giving every child with the phenomenon who was operated on high-dose methylprednisolone (5 to 6 mg/kg a day), a haemostatic or immunoglobulin before surgery, and its abstract says 89% of those operated on had high-dose methylprednisolone beforehand. Prednisolone is also the add-on in the randomised trial of sirolimus. The review notes that the 2013 consensus recommendations of corticosteroids, vincristine or both rest on expert opinion rather than rigorous clinical studies. Long-term use brings temporary growth retardation, a higher risk of infection and behavioural change, and the 21-child series, citing earlier work, adds hypertension, sleep disturbance and hyperglycaemia; so the review advises weaning them as soon as medically feasible, and the VASCERN-VASCA pathway tapering and stopping them once the phenomenon has resolved and the child is stable.

In a cohort of 29 such patients, selected because they had it and had never had the phenomenon, it appeared within 2 years of onset in 72.4%, while 8 did not have it at the first evaluation and developed it later, and only 2 had it before the age of 12 months. Of the 29 lesions, 26 involved the limbs; of all 29, 10 were mixed-type lesions that infiltrated deeply into muscle, bone and joints and 17 were confined to the muscle, bone and joint regions; the knee was the joint most often involved, then the shoulder and hip. Decreased motion also occurred in several patients who attained partial tumour involution. The authors note that its cause is uncertain; citing earlier work, they state that tumour infiltration of muscle, connective tissue and joint structures can lead to diffuse muscle fibrosis and joint contracture. nodes.description: The tumour grows as infiltrating nodules of spindled endothelial cells lining slit-like or crescentic vessels. The endothelium stains for CD31 and CD34 and for the lymphatic markers LYVE1, PROX1 and podoplanin (D2-40), and not for GLUT-1. Angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis are dysregulated and progressive. How fast the endothelium proliferates is not settled: the cohort of 70 reports Ki-67 on the endothelial cells, while in the lesion the 2020 review illustrates only a few nuclei stained for it. The 2020 review adds VEGFR-3 to these lymphatic markers; in a thoracic series of 7 KHEs and 6 kaposiform lymphangiomatoses, all lesions examined had spindle tumour cells staining for CD31 and D2-40, and CD31-positive cells isolated from three of six patients' tumours carried CD31, Ki-67 and LYVE1 in culture. Which signals drive the programme is not established. The review suggests, from the expression of both in KHE, that the VEGF-C/VEGFR3 axis may contribute to the tumour's aggressive behaviour, while serum VEGF-C was lower in KHE patients with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, a different compartment from the tissue, against a comparison group the abstract does not state. Serum angiopoietin-2 was 14-fold raised in KHE when the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon was present and not when it was absent, and the serum study proposes it, with the angiopoietin-1 that was lower alongside VEGF-C, as a marker of the phenomenon's coagulopathy. The review offers vascular remodelling, such as vessel sprouting and inflammatory lymphangiogenesis, as a possible explanation of the rise, raises the possibility of a paracrine effect on the tumour's endothelial cells, and also raises the possibility of a role for angiopoietin-2 in the phenomenon itself.

In a randomised trial in KHE with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, in which sirolimus was given for at least 12 months, adding a short course of prednisolone raised the week-4 platelet response from 24 of 36 to 35 of 37; in a randomised trial in KHE without the phenomenon, low-dose sirolimus was non-inferior to high-dose at one year (about 90% response in both); in a cohort of 167 patients, 92.2% had a durable response. On dose, a series of 21 patients, started on sirolimus alone at 0.8 mg/m2 twice a day once there was no sign of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon aiming for a trough of 5 to 20 ng/mL, found faster tumour shrinkage above a trough of 10 ng/mL and no further gain above 15, in groups of 8, 7 and 6 patients; the randomised trial in KHE without the phenomenon found a trough of 5 to 8 ng/mL non-inferior to 10 to 15 for a volume reduction of at least 20% at month 12, with similar total and serious adverse events but fewer respiratory, skin and mucosal ones. In a pharmacokinetic model of 17 children aged 0.2 to 6 years, the drug's apparent clearance rose with age and was higher in boys than in girls of the same age, which the authors put down to body weight. In the patients with the phenomenon in a 52-patient series, tumour shrinkage did not differ significantly between the 21 given short-term prednisolone for severe symptoms and those on sirolimus alone, whereas the randomised prednisolone trial in KHE with the phenomenon reported better objective lesion responses at month 12 with it. On stopping, rebound growth followed discontinuation in 17.3% of the patients of the cohort of 167 who stopped sirolimus (the abstract does not say how many stopped), associated with early discontinuation and with mixed lesion type, for which the abstract's own confidence interval includes 1; in a series of 26, 25 of them with the phenomenon, 20 completed a course of 28.3 months on average, and the series had no recurrence over a median follow-up of 32 months (the abstract does not say whether follow-up ran from the start or the end of treatment). In the cohort of 167, nonresponse, relapse and long-term sequelae remained despite intensified and prolonged treatment. On harms, serious adverse events were most common in the first year and long-term treatment brought no unacceptable cumulative toxicity in that cohort; in the randomised prednisolone trial, total and grade 3-4 adverse events were similar with and without prednisolone; no patient in the 52-patient series stopped permanently for toxicity, and the 26-patient series reported mild side effects; and a 4-month-old on sirolimus and a prednisolone taper developed Pneumocystis pneumonia with respiratory failure needing extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, after which the authors advise considering prophylaxis.

nodes.description: Complete resection is an option where it can be done safely, but surgery is rarely an option for extensive tumours or where it would badly impair function. The VASCERN-VASCA pathway says radical surgery that avoids functional defects and mutilation can be curative for the rare small tumour without the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, and after failed medical treatment reserves surgery for the rare tumours that can be removed completely without mutilation. Elective resection during the active phenomenon is ill advised: these young children, with very vascular tumours, are at higher risk of blood loss, iatrogenic injury and a worse coagulopathy. The review also cites evidence that manipulating the tumour, by surgery or trauma, can set off the phenomenon, whether or not the child has had it before. Surgery can also remove a fibrofatty residuum or reconstruct damaged structures. Both cited series nonetheless operated on children with the phenomenon. In one single-centre cohort, where over 90% were operated on, the authors favoured early surgery; all 8 low-risk patients recovered after surgery without recurrence, and 6 cases (9%) recurred after a few months as small lesions. In a single-centre series of 21 children, 6 tumours were excised, and the phenomenon resolved within 24 hours of the operation in the 2 of them with the severe Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon.

nodes.description: A vinca alkaloid, given intravenously at 0.05 mg/kg once a week in the 2020 review's table, through a central line. Consensus-derived guidelines recommended vincristine, with or without corticosteroids, as first-line treatment of KHE with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, and the review notes that the 2013 consensus recommendations of corticosteroids, vincristine or both rest on expert opinion rather than rigorous clinical studies; the review now considers sirolimus with corticosteroids a first-line therapy (versus vincristine with corticosteroids); many clinicians and families prefer sirolimus because vincristine needs a central line; and a 21-child series says sirolimus has superseded it in many centres. The VASCERN-VASCA pathway adds vincristine when a lesion compresses vital structures or lies in a life-threatening site, or when sirolimus and corticosteroids fail; notes that, once the diagnosis has been re-confirmed, adding it can shrink a tumour without the phenomenon that has not responded; and allows stopping it once the lesion no longer shrinks. First-line vincristine has an overall response rate of 72%; in a multicentre cohort that pools KHE with tufted angioma, its radiological response at three months was higher than sirolimus's, with no difference at six. In the single-centre series of 21 children, 16 were treated with vincristine, weekly for 6 to 12 weeks and then less often, for a median total of 185 days: 11 needed no other treatment, 3 moved on to sirolimus, and there were no recurrences over a median follow-up of 6.1 years; the series acknowledges an institutional preference for vincristine. The review cites mounting evidence that vincristine alone fails in very severe disease, while in that series the 3 children with the severe Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon who began vincristine had the phenomenon resolve after two doses, alongside supportive measures; one of them later moved to sirolimus. Complications there were common but, in the authors' words, mild in most: 15 of 16 had at least one, 13 were admitted with a febrile illness, 8 had what the authors call bone marrow suppression (a haemoglobin below 100 g/L, managed with iron), 6 had poor weight gain or growth, one of them admitted for tube feeding, 3 central lines were removed early, and 2 children had possible neuropathy, a transient ptosis. Another cohort, citing earlier work, says vincristine is given to children with the phenomenon who do not respond to corticosteroids, but is not used routinely because of its complications, among them myelosuppression in neonates, peripheral neuropathy, constipation and intestinal obstruction.

evidence.snippet: Thirteen (81%) had at least one febrile illness, three of which were neutropenic, and all prompted the protocolised response of admission, blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics.

evidence.reference_title: Management of Kaposiform Haemangioendothelioma-A Retrospective Case Series Examining the Use and Effectiveness of Vincristine.
evidence.snippet: Eight (50%) had documented bone marrow suppression based on the haemoglobin of < 100 g/L, all managed with iron supplementation and none requiring blood product transfusions outside of initial management of their KMP.

evidence.snippet: There were three (19%) central line complications requiring earlier than planned removal: one due to blockage; one due to displacement; and the other due to recurrent entry site cellulitis.

evidence.reference_title: Management of Kaposiform Haemangioendothelioma-A Retrospective Case Series Examining the Use and Effectiveness of Vincristine.
evidence.snippet: Two (13%) developed possible vincristine-related neuropathy: both a transient ptosis which recovered after increasing dosing intervals; one of whom also had sensory axonal neuropathy on nerve conduction studies.
